text: They can't just infinitly eat each others' limbs off... the energy and nutrients to regrow the limbs had to come from somewhere... and they still need energy to move around and for their heart beat. Let's say they need 10 calories a day for their heart beat... and that a limb provides 100 calories. That limb will give them 10 days of calories to survive on. Now, if they want to regrow a limb, it'll take 100 calories, plus the necessary protein & fat to build the tissues. They now need another 100 calories plus protein and fat... So if they want to survive 20 days and regrow a limb, they'll need 300 calories. If they want to live a month, they'll need 300 calories... hat's three limbs eaten and none grown. Where are they going to get all these limbs from?? Well they eat each other, basically.

text: You did mention that they will go cannibalistic, and they will specifically target limbs. However, this would not be an infinite food glitch since the energy required to regrow the limbs is much higher than the caloric value of the eaten limb. So sure it'll help in a pinch to stave off immediate starvation, but it's not a solution to overall lack in food. Axolotl would be much more evolutionarily sound if they weren't completely and utterly carnivorous, they can't even temporarily shift to an omnivorous diet, like most other carnivores, because their digestive system cannot process plants, vegetables, or fruits AT ALL. text:
Fun fact about axolotls. They are just a kind of salamander which evolved to remain in a juvenile state for their entire life (in the right conditions), which gives them the ability to regenerate body parts so easily.

However, if they are left on land for long enough, they will eventually undergo the metamorphosis necessary to develop the traits of a land dwelling salamander, at which point they will look almost indistinguishable from other salamanders, but also lose their enhanced healing ability.

Essentially, they are kid lizars that God told to stop losing half their head on the playground, and to "grow up", and they just said "Nah, I'm good. Oh cool, scissors! Wanna see how fast I can swim with them?"

text:
1. I'd expect a creature that lives in water to have gills.
2. It's not weird. All amphibians have this trait.
3. Yes, they can regenerate everything. Many other salamanders can also just not to this degree.
4. It's not indestructable and the regenerating takes time like any healing.
5. Most creatures use canabalism as a way to escape starvation and they likely don't do it knowing it will regenerate. They do it because they see food and eat it.
6. The regeneration takes a lot of energy like all healing so it's not an infinite food glitch.
7. It's not evil or genius. It's nature and instinct.
Everything about the axolotl makes sense.

They can regenerate because they are akin to a caterpillar in its cocoon, the legs are not done developing yet, so if they get chopped off it just restarts the process that is still ongoing, unlike us who's arms are 100% developed in the Womb and the creation process shuts down. The Axolotl's Gills work by  extracting oxygen from the water, with the movement of the gills helping to circulate water and enhance gas exchange, breathing through their skin is also possible because of diffusion, oxygen diffuses from the water into their blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out, aided by their thin, permeable skin and countercurrent exchange, another example of a skin-breathing organism would be a worm, they need to be moist to survive, oxygen from the environment enters through their skin and carbon dioxide diffuses out

text:
The part of Mexico they live naturally is being detroyed by pollution and the spread of humans into their habitats, drying them up.  And they live in a very small and specific part of the country, in lakes.  So its not like theres a ton of habitat to go around to begin with.  They have a lot that live in labs, but their breeding pool is suffering from lack of diversity in DNA (i.e., the family tree looks like a bush if ya know what I mean) 

Their unique traits make them very important for medical sciences, for reasons you can surely imagine.  It's very important that we dont destroy this special, particularly cute looking species.

Not that I expect this comment section to be their personal saviors or anything, I just wanted to spread awareness while we're here.

text:
1) they’re salamanders so they fall under the amphibian category 
does it go from all water habitat lifestyle to land dwelling? Yes. Is water a low oxygen environment. yes. 

An axolotl doesn’t NATURALLY become land dwelling they prefer water and don’t migrate - however they can become land dwelling by metamorphosis 

In doing so they will loose their gills and develop lungs and loose the fin on their tails. (Like how a tadpole becomes a frog- it develops lungs and its tail recedes) 

When in water they will always stay in a juvenile state of being as they’re paedomorphic (having juvenile aspects as adults) 

all of those things that are amphibians will breathe through their skin. Frogs toads salamanders etc all breathe through skin. It’s cutaneous respiration. 

2) when wounded the new cells that grow are blastema 

Humans get a cut and we have blood cover the wound and oxidize as new skin cells generate - an axolotl in an all water environment that has low oxygen uses blastema cells to stop the injury and heal. 

These cells are ‘generic’ any part of the body be it skin bone muscle spinal brain will get blastema cells, from these cells it can differentiate into whatever tissue etc it needs to be. And regrows from there. This also means that there’s 0 scar tissue. 

Because there’s not old and new cells  side by side just new cells in general.

It diminishes with age and is not indefinite, especially if the injury is repeated. They have simple biology but there’s limits. 

The first time sure the blastema knows what to do - a thing was there it looked like this it did this… but over and over again and it doesn’t quite remember exactly what it should do in layman’s terms.

It can be an issue with fibrotic material we don’t really know. They also have issues with healing their brains. While they can do it, it doesn’t always heal great. 

3) they are really stupid - to be fair they don’t need to be smart to survive they do they’re thing and they’re good enough at it. 

They don’t have a concept of good or evil or probably any real concepts of anything. 

Because of that I don’t think it can be argued that their actions are good and evil since they realizing they’re even a living creature would be wild. 

They are somewhat territorial to other axolotl that are bigger/smaller so they atleast barely understand size/what they are. (But I don’t think they understand that life is a concept) 

And cannibalism goes back from when they’re in an egg just born growing bigger getting older eating others and continuing to be max size and age. 

So eating an arm or leg really doesn’t matter when you eat the eggs the babies the siblings the smaller other axolotl or random stuff like a worm you found or that slapped into your face and you missed 20 times. It’s sort of anything goes and if you’re hungry eat.

text:
I actually have one as a pet, he’s (as I make this comment) my pfp. But there’s a few things wrong with this video, 
For one, axolotls will eat anything that fits in their mouth and it’s an instinctual response, so they don’t consciously choose what they eat very much—they’ll even eat rocks if they brush up on their face. Along with they just aren’t very smart, (not dumb compared to other salamanders but yk) they aren’t consciously aware that other members of their species can grow their limbs back.
They only eat each other’s limbs when they are juveniles but usually don’t when they’re adults as long as they’re in healthy conditions.
They are cannibalistic but not consciously so like the video implies. So nothing about them is “genius” just coincidental.

So overall, this video was poorly researched. No hate to the creator but a rule of thumb that should be followed more: don’t trust creators to give accurate information. Remember, the vast majority don’t make their money by making the information they state 100% accurate. They’re just fine with 5 minutes of googling. So it’s best to not believe what people say online until you research it yourself. If you don’t want to do that then just don’t repeat what you heard to others, or state that it may not be true.

text: The pet trade doesn't actually affect wild axolotls that much, as axolotls have been bred in captivity for decades. Wild axolotls are critically endangered due to invasive species, pollution, and habitat loss, though there are some issues with poaching. Captive axolotls are also very genetically different from wild axolotls and can not safely be released into the wild for a variety of reasons.

author: @SC-pg7jr

text:
​ @SC-pg7jr yes they have approximately 300 eggs in a single batch but this doesn't make them easy to breed. Axolotls in the pet trade are heavily inbred so allowing them to breed without controls in place is highly unethical and leads to genetic abnormalities including deformities, extremely shortened life spans and other health issues
Also, when raising the babies they need separating into separate tanks as soon as they start to grow limbs or they will cannibalise each other which is why most professional breeders only keep about 20 to 30 eggs from a single batch
Lastly, the females can literally be bred to death. If they are not separated from the males they will keep producing eggs until they die of exhaustion
